prompt.context: You are a Starbucks executive. The company is considering launching a new product: soft-serve ice cream across all US stores.
prompt.question: How would you think about launching soft-serve ice cream at Starbucks? Should Starbucks do it?

clarifying_info.q: Does Starbucks have a specific financial goal for this launch?
clarifying_info.a: There is no specific financial goal.

clarifying_info.q: Is this for US stores or worldwide, and all stores or just some?
clarifying_info.a: Consider this for all US stores.

clarifying_info.q: Have any competitors done something like this?
clarifying_info.a: I don't have information, but it's something you can think about.

clarifying_info.q: What kind of ice cream does Starbucks want to introduce?

framework: Customer: Who are Starbucks' customers, what are their preferences, and what is their willingness to pay for ice cream? Consider demographics, psychographics, and overall health/consumption trends.
Market: Who are the competitors (ice cream vendors, specialty desserts, grocery store ice cream, existing Starbucks products)? What is market share concentration and what barriers to entry exist?
Profitability – Revenue: How many customers will buy ice cream and at what price? Is this additive or does it cannibalize existing sales?

Profitability – Costs: Fixed costs (storage equipment, SG&A, marketing, training) and variable costs (raw materials, additional labor). Also consider opportunity costs of pursuing this instead of other initiatives.

questions.prompt: Who is the target customer for Starbucks soft-serve ice cream, and what factors should drive the customer analysis?
questions.guidance: A strong answer segments customers by demographics and psychographics, considers existing Starbucks loyalists vs. new segments, benchmarks willingness to pay against comparable products, and addresses macro trends such as healthier eating, reduced sugar consumption, and growth in specialty/premium desserts.

questions.prompt: How would you assess the market and competitive landscape for this launch?
questions.guidance: Identify relevant competitors: dedicated ice cream chains (e.g., Dairy Queen, Baskin-Robbins), specialty dessert shops, grocery store ice cream, and Starbucks' own cold/dessert offerings. Evaluate market share concentration and whether Starbucks' brand recognition creates or overcomes barriers to entry. Note that a saturated market with strong incumbents weakens the launch case.

questions.prompt: Walk through a financial analysis to determine whether the ice cream launch is viable. Use per-store daily economics.
questions.guidance: Build a simple per-store P&L. Key steps: estimate daily customer count from hourly traffic and operating hours, estimate daily revenue, apply an ice cream adoption rate while netting out cannibalization, and calculate incremental daily revenue. The structure matters more than the exact numbers.

steps: Daily customers = 200 customers/hr x 10 hrs operating = 2,000 customers/day
Daily revenue baseline = 2,000 customers x $4 avg spend = $8,000/day
Gross ice cream adoption = 5% of customers; cannibalization = 4% of customers; net new = 1%
Incremental daily revenue = 1% x $8,000 = $80/day per store
Optional: compare $80/day to fixed and variable cost of adding ice cream to assess payback
math.answer: $80 in additional revenue per store per day under these assumptions. This should be compared to incremental costs to determine whether the launch is financially justified.

questions.prompt: (Optional) What risks do you see to implementation?
questions.guidance: Employee confusion and additional training time; operational complexity of adding cold equipment; brand confusion (does ice cream fit Starbucks' premium coffee identity?); risk that purchases are mostly one-time rather than building customer lifetime value; potential for cannibalization to exceed projected 4%.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors would you consider when evaluating whether to launch and how to implement?

categories.name: Customer
ideas: Who buys: existing Starbucks regulars vs. new dessert-seeking customers
Willingness to pay: benchmark premium ice cream pricing vs. commodity
Trends: health-conscious consumers reducing sugar; specialty/premium desserts growing
Bundling behavior: customers ordering ice cream alongside coffee

categories.name: Market & Competitive
ideas: Direct competitors: Dairy Queen, Baskin-Robbins, Cold Stone, local shops
Indirect: grocery store pints, Starbucks Frappuccino/cold beverages
Barriers: Starbucks brand strength helps; competitors' loyalty programs are barriers
Market saturation risk in summer/warm climates vs. untapped opportunity in cooler seasons

categories.name: Profitability – Revenue
ideas: Adoption rate above cannibalization rate required for net positive revenue
Bundling with beverages could increase average ticket
Seasonal demand (summer peaks) may create uneven cash flows
Promotional vehicle to drive store traffic even if margin is thin

categories.name: Profitability – Costs
ideas: Capital: soft-serve machines, refrigerated storage, installation
Operating: additional labor for machine operation and cleaning
Training costs and complexity
SG&A and marketing to launch the product
Opportunity cost of capital and counter space vs. other initiatives

categories.name: Implementation & Brand
ideas: Store layout and counter space constraints
Employee training time and operational complexity
Brand alignment: does ice cream strengthen or dilute Starbucks' premium coffee identity?
Pilot in select markets before national rollout to test economics
Supplier selection and cold-chain logistics

recommendation: Launch scenario: If incremental revenue per store per day ($80+) exceeds daily incremental costs, launch soft-serve ice cream — especially if it drives traffic, expands the customer base, and creates promotional value beyond direct margin.

No-launch scenario: If incremental revenue barely covers costs, cannibalization is higher than estimated, or the product risks diluting Starbucks' premium brand identity and existing customer loyalty, do not launch.
risks: Revenue may be lower if cannibalization exceeds 4% or ice cream adoption is below 5%
Operational complexity could reduce service speed and damage core beverage customer satisfaction
Brand confusion if ice cream is perceived as inconsistent with Starbucks' premium positioning
One-time novelty purchases with no repeat behavior would not support ongoing costs
next_steps: Conduct customer research to validate willingness to pay and adoption assumptions
Run a pilot in 20-50 stores across diverse markets to gather real unit economics
Evaluate full cost build-up (capex for equipment, incremental labor, training) against pilot revenue
Assess brand perception impact through customer surveys before national decision
